column11: Megillah 13a: ‘the responsibility of Judah, as David did not kill Shimei, although he was liable to the death penalty. The grave consequences of this failure included that Mordecai was born from him, and it was he against whom Haman was jealous, leading Haman to issue a decree against all of the Jewish people. And how a Benjamite has repaid me is referring to the fact that Saul, who was from the tribe of Benjamin, did not kill the Amalekite king Agag immediately, from whom Haman was later born, and he caused suffering to the Jewish people.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Megillah 13a) to illuminate his argument here (“And likewise concerning Ahasuerus they said (Megillah 13a): "From the censure of that wicked one we learn his praise, in that he did not cohabit by day, etc.", in that he too observed outward decorum in this passion,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And I have received a tradition that the Sanhedrin and all the Men of the Great Assembly of that generation knew the underlying truth, that this was only an outward decree, and they paid no serious heed to it at all; only Mordechai, from whom this inner secret was concealed, was the one who cried out and rallied the people over it; thus I heard.
column15: Therefore man is born without mature knowledge, initially indulging and receiving bounty like the nations, only later coming to praise Hashem even for that youthful experience. Hence the Torah begins from Bereishit: for although in truth conscious awareness is primary before Hashem, the Blessed Name desires to grant Israel the vitality of the nations as well.

column11: Megillah 13b: ‘And what was the modesty shown by Saul? As it is written: “But of the matter of the kingdom, of which Samuel spoke, he did not tell him” (I Samuel 10:16). Saul expressed his modesty by not revealing Samuel’s promise that he would be king, and thereby merited that Esther would descend from him. Similarly, Rabbi Elazar said: When the Holy One, Blessed be He, assigns greatness to a person, He assigns it to his sons and to his son’s sons for all generations, as it is stated: “He withdraws not his eyes from the righteous; but with kings upon the throne He establishes them forever, and they are exalted” (Job 36:7). And if he becomes arrogant due to this, the Holy One, Blessed be He, lowers him…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Megillah 13b) to illuminate his argument here (“as our Sages of blessed memory noted (Megillah 13b) on the verse "Esther had not yet disclosed her people": that all descendants of Rachel are characterized by modesty; and so regarding King Saul our Sages said...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And so too, from Amalek's seed would surely sprout the ultimate instrument of Amalek's eradication and the complete uprooting of his existence. And similarly, the endeavor of teaching Torah to young school children, which addresses the most rudimentary level of intellect, where the teacher contracts his own intellect to match the capacity of the child's understanding.
column15: So creation as a whole yearned to straighten what was crooked after the early generations stumbled, becoming reconciled to exist as an enduring realm distinct from its Source, its foundations stabilized forever. As in Midrash Tehillim (82): The soul seeks every hour to depart the body, so how does it remain?

column11: Esther 2:20: ‘But Esther still did not reveal her kindred or her people, as Mordecai had instructed her; for Esther obeyed Mordecai’s bidding, as she had done when she was under his tutelage.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Esther 2:20) to illuminate his argument here (“on the verse "Esther had not yet disclosed her people": that all descendants of Rachel are characterized by modesty; and so regarding King Saul our Sages said (Berakhot 62b): the modesty you displayed in the cave...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: From the side of Hashem, blessed be He, the foundation is the loftiest and most sublime height, far above the reach of all elevated minds, and this is the Fiftieth Gate concealed from every creature. And to it clings the simple perception of young schoolchildren, which is the most straightforward, unadorned comprehension, in which all hidden, esoteric wisdoms are implicitly contained in its simplicity, which itself constitutes absolute truth.
column15: The explanation is that at that point existence was still enfolded in pure Thought, the inception of creation commencing from “Bereishit,” as the Sages taught: “Bereishit is also an utterance.” And the utterance “Bereishit” corresponds to Job 28:27–28: “Then He saw it and declared it; He prepared it, and searched it out; and unto man He said,” meaning that the divine concepts of Torah cascaded from the Emanator through this evolutionary descent until reaching human perception, which is “and unto man He said.”

column11: Berakhot 62b: ‘And what is this modesty? As it is written: “And he came to the sheepcotes by the way, where there was a cave, and Saul went in to cover his feet, to defecate. Now David and his men were sitting in the innermost parts of the cave” (I Samuel 24:3). It was taught that the Sages said: There was a fence within a fence, and a cave within a cave, and Saul entered to defecate in the interest of modesty. With regard to the use of the term, to cover his feet, Rabbi Elazar said: This teaches that, even there, he covered himself with his garment like a sukka.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 62b) to illuminate his argument here (“and so regarding King Saul our Sages said (Berakhot 62b): the modesty you displayed in the cave spared your life; for this is their quintessential trait in silence and privacy, wherefore Esther reigned over the Persians,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And all forms of wisdom are there manifest within the plain truth itself; and this is identical to the pure perception of young schoolchildren. The difference lies not in the core essence of that perception, but merely in the degree of its expansion: for the attainment of the hidden mysteries within the perception of schoolchildren is completely cloaked in concealment, while in the Fiftieth Gate—all is revealed.
column15: And to comprehend the structural shift in Genesis: why prior to Shabbat the text employs the term “Beriah” (creation), whereas after Shabbat it employs “Yetzirah” (formation): Because these represent two distinct phases in the cosmic cascading of reality, step by step, enclothing supernal light within garment upon garment; as in the Zohar (Balak 204b): The primordial light shone so brilliantly that worlds could not endure it; what did the Holy One do? He fashioned light within light to enclothe one within the other.

column11: Kiddushin 21b: ‘The Sages taught: With regard to a beautiful captive, the verse states: “And sees among the captives,” teaching that this halakha applies only if he notices her when she is a captive. The expression “a woman” teaches that she is permitted even if she is a married woman. The phrase “a beautiful woman” indicates that the Torah here spoke only in response to the evil inclination, as it is due to her beauty that he desired her. And why does the Torah permit this? It is preferable for Jews to eat the meat’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Kiddushin 21b) to illuminate his argument here (“our Sages of blessed memory noted (Kiddushin 21b): the Torah spoke solely facing the raging evil inclination, and not out of any inherent sanctity, for in that union there is no reception of holiness.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And seeing that in the end she converts, he assumed it was completely permissible. Yet in truth "the Torah spoke solely to counter the yetzer hara" (Kiddushin 21b); and even though she departs from being a harlot once she converts and becomes a God-fearing woman; nevertheless, since her conversion is not entirely voluntary, but for the sake of a husband or under duress; mirroring the Samaritan converts out of fear of lions: "They feared Hashem, and served their own gods" (II Melachim 17:33).
column15: For once Hashem chose Jacob and cut His covenant with him, He desires the enduring preservation of Israel, not their total dissolution. Even the commandment of sanctifying the Name (Kiddush Hashem)—where one must surrender life for His holiness—applies only in public before ten Jews, where an enduring legacy remains as God’s Name is magnified publicly, etching holiness in the hearts of onlookers.

column13: And initially the five occurrences of light in the utterance 'Let there be light' correspond to the Five Books of the Torah (Bereishit Rabbah), and subsequently the Primordial Light was concealed for those who toil in the Oral Torah (Midrash Tanchuma, Noach ibid.); and regarding the Oral Torah Scripture proclaims: 'My speech shall distill as the dew' (Deuteronomy 32:2), and as we explained, the Oral Torah resembles dew which is not visibly noticed as descending from heaven.

column11: Pirkei Avot 3:17: ‘Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah said: Where there is no Torah, there is no right conduct; where there is no right conduct, there is no Torah. Where there is no wisdom, there is no fear of God; where there is no fear of God, there is no wisdom. Where there is no understanding, there is no knowledge; where there is no knowledge, there is no understanding. Where there is no bread, there is no Torah; where there is no Torah, there is no bread. He used to say: one whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, to what may he be compared? To a tree whose branches are numerous but whose roots are few, so that when the wind comes, it uproots it and overturns it, as it is said, “He shall be like a bush in the desert,…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Pirkei Avot 3:17) to illuminate his argument here (“And our Sages of blessed memory (Avot 3:17) allegorized this to a tree whose roots are deep and abundant; meaning that Israel are rooted in the Three Patriarchs, 'the unyielding rocks, the foundations of the earth'....”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And this matches Avot (3:17): "If there is no wisdom there is no fear; if there is no fear there is no wisdom," Awe being the discipline within deeds to become fearful of sin. And "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom" (Job 28:28), for the one cannot endure without the other. And rash (destitute) is the inverse of rosh (head), the latter spelled with an Aleph denoting the Sovereign (Aluph) of the Universe concealed within it.
column15: Understanding that man must conduct himself with awe, balancing soul and time (the Vavs uniting seasons, saving from abundance for adversity, putting collective good over selfish gain) — they schemed to erect an occult monument where the Flood victims had settled, hoping to generate automatic, unreflective dread to bypass personal moral exertion.

He who subdues his inclination," which is achieved through the fear of Heaven that restrains his spirit, as noted above [and the spirit (Ruach) resides in the heart, as written elsewhere regarding the tripartite soul: Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah].
column15: Meaning that the Blessed Name desires to give Israel every mitzvah and holy deed from its primordial root, so that even beyond conscious intellect they may attain the sanctity of the Patriarchs. And this is “He declared the power of His works to His people”—that the Blessed Name imparted to His people the inward vitality and soul of every holy action.

column13: Thus the overarching root of the pursuing Amalek inverts into being pursued by his own device; so that the decree Haman wrote "that the Jews should be ready for that day", the interpretation became inverted as clarified in the second royal letters, the intent becoming that the Jews should rule over their adversaries; and the gallows he prepared for Mordechai inverted into being erected for him; meaning that the initial triumph of the imagination itself later turned inside out.
column15: The rationale being: during weekdays, even as man expands within the garment, a minute memory of the inner essence remains preserved; but were he to finalize the outer garment on the Sabbath day, he would completely forget the divine Root that animates it, clinging to an alienated shell.

column13: And it is scheduled prior to Pesach, in order to merit through it on Pesach the Resurrection of the Dead which will unfold on Pesach; wherefore on the intermediate Sabbath of Pesach we read as the Haftarah the vision of the Dry Bones (Yechezkel 37).
column15: Therefore one who partakes of physical bounty as the nations do, taking without restraint and without a blessing— which alludes to the years of youthful expansiveness in a person before attaining maturity— and afterward the Blessed Name grants him the conscious wisdom to praise Him for it; for upon sight alone one does not recite a blessing over sustenance, but only upon tasting, even though while tasting one is momentarily distracted.

column11: Esther 9:1: ‘And so, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month—that is, the month of Adar—when the king’s command and decree were to be executed, the very day on which the enemies of the Jews had expected to get them in their power, the opposite happened, and the Jews got their enemies in their power.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Esther 9:1) to illuminate his argument here (“then it was demonstrated that 'it was turned to the contrary, that the Jews had rule over those who hated them, etc.' And Haman boasted: "Yea, Esther the queen did let no man come in, etc.", presuming this was...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And the salvations of the blessed Hashem traverse all the worlds until they clothe themselves even in the physical World of Action, bringing rescue to physical bodies as well. Hence the enduring impression established for all generations could likewise be committed to writing and clothed within the letters of the text; and likewise festivals were established from them, celebrated through bodily pleasure, joy, and cessation of labor, because salvation was effected for the physical body as well.
column15: Scheming to bind all to that single righteous soul sealed by Hashem, claiming a share in his inviolable standing, since the power of the whole resides in each part. Yet Hashem demonstrated that no scheme can coerce the supreme Will through stubborn force: for Abraham was singular, chosen by Hashem as the spark of life of those generations, and he separated from their conspiracy, refusing to join their plot (Bereishit Rabbah 38:13).

Thus his entire...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And from the side of this world, even the words of the opinion there [Berachos 34b] — that all the prophets prophesied only for baalei teshuvah, etc. — are true, for “these and those are the words of the living God.” And from the side of what is apprehended by the prophets, the rank of the baalei teshuvah is lower than the completely righteous — for this rung of teshuvah is not apprehended from the side of prophecy at all, as R’ Yochanan himself said there, “all the prophets prophesied only for the days of Mashiach, but of the World to Come, ‘no eye has seen a God besides You who acts for the one who waits for Him’ (Yeshayah 64:3).”
column15: The meaning is: the question was, how could such pitch darkness fall upon Israel as in the days of Haman, spawning such terror that they thought they would be utterly obliterated, heaven forbid, when they well knew Hashem bound His very Name to Israel, giving them the unbreakable plea: “What will You do for Your great Name!”?

column11: Esther Rabbah 6:12: ‘“Esther did not disclose her family or her people, as Mordekhai had commanded her; Esther followed Mordekhai’s instructions, as it was when she was fostered by him” (Esther 2:20).“Esther did not disclose her family” – teaching that she practiced silence for herself, like her ancestor Rachel, who practiced the craft of silence; all her great descendants maintained silence. Rachel adopted the craft of silence – she saw her betrothal gifts in the possession of her sister and she was silent. Benjamin her son practiced silence – know, as his stone in the breast piece was a chalcedony [yashefe], [i.e.,] he had a mouth [yesh peh], but was silent. Saul, her grandson – “but the matter of the…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Esther Rabbah 6:12) to illuminate his argument here (“as our Sages of blessed memory noted (Esther Rabbah 6:12); and so in the end, through this she merited the Holy Spirit, and seemingly the authorship of the Megillah was established through her as well, as it is...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: For when through the conquest of evil the glory of Heaven is elevated, even the essence of evil is elevated back to its primeval origin, which is the very purpose for which evil was created: that man conquer it and thereby disclose the glory of Heaven. But with Saul it was termed merely "putting evil to the worse", for the spiritual treatise animating his warfare was never unveiled; it remained known to him alone, leaving no lasting manifest impact in deed.

column13: So too, the perception of school children, which is the simplest and most elementary attainment, enables them to learn directly from the mouth of the Holy One; in the sense of the verse: “From the mouths of babes and sucklings You established strength,” for through them the bedrock of Torah is built from below upward; the foundation is set at the lowest point below.
column15: In Space (Olam) exist the six attributes doubled from above to below and below to above—the twelve supernal showbreads (Sha'ar HaKavanot); And as the Arizal, of blessed memory, wrote (Sha’ar HaKavanot, on the subject of the table, Friday night): “With vavs it is bound, and the species of the assemblies.”

column11: Megillah 6b: ‘The Gemara asks: Is that so? Didn’t Rabbi Yoḥanan say in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai: It is permitted to provoke the wicked in this world, as it is stated: “They that forsake the Torah praise the wicked; but they who keep the Torah contend with them” (Proverbs 28:4)? And furthermore, it is taught in a baraita that Rabbi Dostai bar Matun said: It is permitted to provoke the wicked in this world, and if a person whispers to you to say that this is not so, relying on the verse: “Contend not with evildoers, nor be envious against the workers of iniquity” (Psalms 37:1), know that only one whose heart strikes him with pangs of conscience over sins that he committed says this.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Megillah 6b) to illuminate his argument here (“And this is the principle of 'juxtaposing redemption to redemption' (Megillah 6b): that Nisan is the inception of Israel's redemption, wherein they were consecrated as a unique people by virtue of their being walled...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: So too, the final fruition of a sacred deed is not in mortal hands alone, as taught in Megillah (6b): to retain one's learning requires Heavenly assistance (Siyata DiShmaya); and in Sanhedrin (93b): "'and Hashem was with him'—teaching that the halachah was established in accordance with David everywhere"; meaning that every practical outcome resulting from his wisdom and understanding aligned flawlessly with true halachah solely because Hashem was with him.
column15: And all this exists through the veil of concealment, wherein man perceives himself as an autonomous entity. And such was Hashem's desire in creating the cosmos: that man should feel separate, recognizing himself as a creature; and this is signified by the name Enosh, meaning frailty and weakness, as written (Psalms 9:21): “Let the nations know that they are but men (enosh), Selah.”

The Gemara asks: That works out well according to the one who said: Permission was granted to write the Scroll of Esther in the Bible as a book whose sanctity equals that of the other books of the Bible. However, according to the one who said: Permission was not granted to write the Scroll of Esther in the Bible, and its sanctity does…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 29a) to illuminate his argument here (“as our Sages of blessed memory taught in Yoma (29a), and the written text represents that which is openly manifest to all, unlike that which remains oral; wherefore they taught in Midrash Rabbah (Ki Tisa 47:1;...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.

column15: And this explains Yoma (9b): “Regarding the Second Temple, whose sin was not openly manifest, their end of exile was not revealed; and why were they exiled? Because of baseless hatred (sin'at chinam).” And this was the very reason their redemption was hidden: because they ruined in practical action the root of unity through baseless hatred, they forfeited the primordial sanctity of the Temple and were exiled.

For emotional feeling in the heart leads to burning excitation until one cannot function, whereas through rational recognition in thought one does not burn with excitement, and acts properly with calm composure; only that it proceeds by way of habit and custom, since he lacks emotional feeling in the heart.

column15: Yet after creation suffered through the shattering of ten worlds and the screening of light through Ten Utterances, investing toil into preserving existence — one who damages the world now harms his fellow human beings, unpardonable until he appeases his fellow (Yoma 85b), having ruined a vast edifice raised through the agony of shattered worlds and human exertion.

column11: Zohar, Eikev 4:50-61: “In the Zohar (Eikev III 273b), it is taught that no generation in Israel ever contains fewer than six hundred thousand souls—corresponding to the six hundred thousand root letters of the Torah.” Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Eikev 4:50-61) to illuminate his argument here (“as our Sages stated (Zohar Part III, 273b): no generation consists of fewer than sixty myriad; and so they said in Berakhot (58a): "there is no full populace (okhlasa) fewer than sixty myriad"; and including the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Nonetheless, from the perspective of bodily generation breath is higher, the voice merely maintaining its existence, whereas breath possesses expansive generative power to give birth to voice, being its primeval root]. Therefore at that very moment the Eagle arrived—which is his heavenly assistance, identical with that subtle breath in Parashat Bo which was the root of his aid—and through it he beheld whatever he beheld and flew four hundred parasangs, meaning the entire extent of the Land of Israel, which encompasses all bodily faculties, until he reached the Mountains of Darkness.
column15: Hence it says “If you restrain your foot because of the Sabbath,” warning against further expansion into outer garments, returning instead to the Root stripped of all clothing, as the Holy Zohar taught: “he must attend solely unto Him and to no other.”
